learning_goal: Place the hippocampus in the floor of the INFERIOR HORN of the lateral ventricle and let everything else follow from that one position. Because it lies in a ventricle it is curved, paired, and has an output that has to travel a long way round to reach the front of the brain — the FORNIX, arching under the corpus callosum to the mammillary body. Because it is deep in the medial temporal lobe it is the first thing a temporal mass, a herniation or a hypoxic insult reaches. And because its job is CONSOLIDATION rather than storage, a bilateral lesion gives dense anterograde amnesia with old memories and skills intact — the single most examined fact in this topic, and one the geometry explains rather than decorates.

structures.name: left hippocampus
structures.label: Hippocampus (L)
structures.narration: A curved ridge of cortex rolled into the floor of the INFERIOR (temporal) HORN of the lateral ventricle, running front to back through the medial temporal lobe with its head bulging forward under the uncus. It is cortex, not a nucleus — three-layered allocortex folded on itself, so a coronal section through it shows two interlocking C's, Ammon's horn and the dentate gyrus. The shape is worth holding because it is the reason the output leaves BACKWARDS: fibres gather on its ventricular surface as the fimbria, which continues as the crus of the fornix, so the road out of the hippocampus starts at the back of a structure whose target lies at the front.

structures.name: right hippocampus
structures.label: Hippocampus (R)
structures.narration: The mirror of the left, and the pairing is the clinical point rather than a symmetry note. ONE hippocampus can be removed — as it is in surgery for drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy — with a material-specific memory deficit rather than amnesia. It takes BOTH to produce the dense anterograde amnesia the topic is famous for, which is why the injuries that do it are the ones that hit the medial temporal lobes on both sides at once: hypoxia, herpes simplex encephalitis, and bilateral surgery. Verbal material leans left and visuospatial material leans right in most people, which is what 'material-specific' means at the bedside.

structures.name: left parahippocampal gyrus
structures.label: Parahippocampal gyrus (L)
structures.narration: The gyrus on the medial surface of the temporal lobe that the hippocampus is rolled into, and the doorway through which nearly all cortical input reaches it: its anterior part is the ENTORHINAL cortex, whose perforant path is the hippocampus's principal afferent. Its front end hooks medially as the UNCUS, and that hook sits directly over the edge of the tentorium beside the midbrain — so a temporal mass pushes the uncus through the tentorial notch and compresses the third nerve and the midbrain. The same medial temporal position that makes this the memory gateway makes it the herniation site.

structures.name: right parahippocampal gyrus
structures.label: Parahippocampal gyrus (R)
structures.narration: The right-sided partner, shown so the pair can be read together on the underside of the brain. Both parahippocampal gyri are lit in beat 2 because the medial temporal region is a bilateral structure clinically: it is the bilateral insult that causes amnesia, and it is the uncus on the side of an expanding mass that herniates.

structures.name: left lateral ventricle
structures.label: Lateral ventricle (L)
structures.narration: The ventricle is context here and it is the single most useful piece of context in the scene: the hippocampus is IN its inferior horn, in the floor, and the fornix runs along the ventricular system all the way forward. Find the temporal horn on a coronal MRI and the grey ridge in its floor is the hippocampus — that is how mesial temporal sclerosis is read, as a small hippocampus with a widened temporal horn beside it.

structures.name: right lateral ventricle
structures.label: Lateral ventricle (R)
structures.narration: The right ventricle, shown for the same reason as the left: the two temporal horns are the landmarks the hippocampi are read against, and asymmetry between them is the finding. `ventricular-system-csf__ventricles` owns the ventricular system itself; this scene borrows only the inferior horn.

structures.name: left fornix of forebrain
structures.label: Fornix (L)
structures.narration: The output. Fibres leave the hippocampus as the fimbria on its ventricular surface, sweep back and up as the CRUS of the fornix under the splenium of the corpus callosum, run forward as the BODY of the fornix under the callosum, and turn down in front of the third ventricle as the COLUMN. The column then divides at the anterior commissure, and it is the POSTCOMMISSURAL half — the fibres passing behind the commissure — that ends in the MAMMILLARY BODY and carries Papez; the precommissural half goes to the septal region instead. `limbic-system__fornix-papez-circuit` owns that split in full. It is a long arch to reach a target that sits only a few centimetres from where it started, and it is long because it has to get out of a ventricle and over a thalamus to do it. Follow it once in 3D and the Papez circuit stops being a list.

structures.name: right fornix of forebrain
structures.label: Fornix (R)
structures.narration: The right arch, identical in course. Seen from the side the two fornices look like one structure; seen from above they are a pair of arches that converge in the midline as they run forward, which is the arrangement the commissure sits in.

structures.name: commissure of fornix of forebrain
structures.label: Commissure of the fornix
structures.narration: Where the two crura come together under the splenium, fibres cross between them — the hippocampal commissure, the psalterium. It matters for one reason worth stating plainly: the two hippocampi are directly connected, so a seizure focus in one medial temporal lobe has a short route to the other, and bilateral independent foci are common in long-standing temporal lobe epilepsy.

structures.name: mammillary body
structures.label: Mammillary body
structures.narration: The destination of the POSTCOMMISSURAL column of the fornix, a small paired swelling on the underside of the hypothalamus behind the tuber cinereum. It is the hinge of the Papez circuit: hippocampus to fornix to mammillary body, mammillary body to anterior thalamic nucleus by the mammillothalamic tract, thalamus to cingulate gyrus, cingulate back to the parahippocampal gyrus and into the hippocampus again. The mammillary bodies are also where THIAMINE deficiency does its damage, which is why Korsakoff's amnesia looks like a hippocampal amnesia without a hippocampal lesion — the circuit is cut at the hinge rather than at the start. Atrophic mammillary bodies on MRI are the chronic sign.

structures.name: left thalamus
structures.label: Thalamus (L)
structures.narration: Shown as the next station and as the obstacle the fornix arches over. The relevant part is the ANTERIOR nucleus, which is not separately modelled here — the whole thalamus is lit and the narration says which corner of it is meant, rather than pretending the nucleus is drawn. `basal-ganglia-diencephalon__thalamus` owns the nuclei.

structures.name: right thalamus
structures.label: Thalamus (R)
structures.narration: The right thalamus, for the same reason. Note the sides while both are lit: FMA258716 is the LEFT thalamus and FMA258714 the RIGHT — the ids are one character apart and the catalog names, not the numbers, are what settle it.

structures.name: left cingulate gyrus
structures.label: Cingulate gyrus (L)
structures.narration: The arch of cortex over the corpus callosum that carries the circuit back. Thalamus to cingulate, cingulate along the cingulum bundle to the parahippocampal gyrus, and into the hippocampus — the loop is closed. Seen in 3D the cingulate gyrus and the fornix are two concentric arches around the callosum, the fornix inside and the cingulate outside, and that picture is the whole of Papez in one image.

structures.name: right cingulate gyrus
structures.label: Cingulate gyrus (R)
structures.narration: The right arch. Both are shown in the mechanism beats so the circuit can be traced on one side while the other stays visible as its mirror.

structures.name: corpus callosum
structures.label: Corpus callosum
structures.narration: Context and a landmark rather than a limbic structure. The fornix runs under it and the cingulate gyrus over it, and the crura of the fornix and their commissure sit under its SPLENIUM — so the callosum is the reference surface that tells you which arch you are looking at. `cerebrum-gross-lobes__white-matter-tracts` owns it.

views.title: In the floor of the temporal horn
views.narration: Start with the position, because every other fact in this scene is a consequence of it. The hippocampus is a curved ridge of cortex lying in the FLOOR OF THE INFERIOR HORN of the lateral ventricle, deep in the medial temporal lobe, running from the head under the uncus backwards and up towards the atrium. The ventricles are ghosted beside it so the relationship reads: hippocampus inside the cavity, not beside it. Two things follow immediately and are used later. It is curved because the ventricle is curved. And it is DEEP and MEDIAL, which is why it is reached by things that come from inside — herniation, hypoxia, viral encephalitis — rather than by a blow to the side of the head.

views.title: The pair, and the gyrus they are rolled into
views.narration: From below, both hippocampi and both parahippocampal gyri together. The gyrus is the surface you can see on the underside of the brain; the hippocampus is what that surface is rolled into, hidden in the ventricle above it. The anterior parahippocampal gyrus is the ENTORHINAL cortex, the funnel through which cortical information reaches the hippocampus, and its hooked front end is the UNCUS lying against the tentorial edge. Note the symmetry — both hippocampi draw here — and then note why it matters: losing ONE hippocampus costs material-specific memory — verbal on the left, visuospatial on the right — while losing BOTH costs the ability to lay down new declarative memory at all.

views.title: A coronal cut through the temporal horn
views.narration: Cut coronally through the middle of the temporal lobes and read the section the way a radiologist reads it: temporal horn as a dark slit, hippocampus as the grey mass in its floor, parahippocampal gyrus below and medial to it, the tentorial edge and the midbrain just medial again. This is the view in which MESIAL TEMPORAL SCLEROSIS is diagnosed — a shrunken, bright hippocampus on one side with the temporal horn dilated to fill the space — and it is the commonest cause of drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy in adults, the reason a hippocampus is ever removed. Be honest about the limit of the geometry: the internal architecture this section would ideally show, Ammon's horn interlocking with the dentate gyrus and the CA1 sector that is most vulnerable to hypoxia, has NO mesh in the catalog. The cut shows the whole hippocampus as one body; the layers inside it are described here and not drawn, and `gaps[]` records that.

views.title: Same cut, one level forward — the uncus at the tentorial edge
views.narration: Move the plane forward to the head of the hippocampus and the uncus comes into the section, hooked medially towards the midline. There is nothing between it and the midbrain but the free edge of the tentorium, and that is the whole anatomy of uncal herniation: a mass anywhere in the hemisphere pushes this hook over the edge, which compresses the third nerve — a blown pupil on the SAME side — and then the midbrain itself. The oculomotor nerve is named and NOT drawn; the catalog contains no cranial nerve except the two optic nerves, and `cranial-nerves__cranial-nerve-courses` owns it. What this beat can genuinely show is why the uncus is the part that goes: it is the most medial point of the temporal lobe and it already overhangs the notch.

views.title: Out along the fornix to the mammillary body
views.narration: Trace the output once, whole. Fibres leave the hippocampus along its ventricular surface as the FIMBRIA, sweep back and up under the splenium as the CRUS, exchange fibres with the other side at the COMMISSURE, run forward under the corpus callosum as the BODY, and dive down in front of the third ventricle as the COLUMN, whose POSTCOMMISSURAL half — the fibres passing behind the anterior commissure — ends in the MAMMILLARY BODY. Say postcommissural once and mean it: the precommissural fibres peel off in front of the commissure to the septal region and are not part of Papez, which is why the flat sentence 'the fornix ends in the mammillary body' is a half-truth. Watch the arch rather than the names: the hippocampus sits in a ventricle at the bottom and back, its target sits at the front and middle, and the fornix is the detour that connects them over the top of the thalamus. The commissure is not decoration — it is the direct link between the two hippocampi, and it is why a temporal lobe seizure focus can seed its partner.

views.title: Papez, closed — two arches around the callosum
views.narration: Now close the loop and look at the shape it makes. Mammillary body up to the ANTERIOR nucleus of the thalamus by the mammillothalamic tract; thalamus to the CINGULATE gyrus; cingulate back along the cingulum to the parahippocampal gyrus; parahippocampal into the hippocampus. Seen from the medial side the circuit is simply two concentric arches around the corpus callosum — the fornix on the inside, the cingulate gyrus on the outside — meeting at each end. Two of the links are described and not drawn, and the beat says so: the mammillothalamic tract and the cingulum bundle have no mesh in this catalog, and the anterior thalamic nucleus is not separable from the whole thalamus that is lit for it. What is drawn is every station; what is described is the wiring between them.

views.title: Why the lesion is amnesia — and which amnesia
views.narration: The hippocampus CONSOLIDATES: it converts experience into durable declarative memory and hands it to the cortex, where it is stored. It is not the store. That distinction is the whole clinical picture and it can be read off the two lit structures. Take out both hippocampi and the patient cannot form new declarative memories — dense ANTEROGRADE amnesia — while childhood memories, vocabulary, and motor skills survive, because those are cortical, and procedural learning runs through the basal ganglia and cerebellum instead. Cut the circuit at its hinge instead, at the MAMMILLARY BODIES, and thiamine deficiency produces a memory disorder that looks much the same: Korsakoff's, with confabulation, following Wernicke's encephalopathy. Same circuit, different point of failure, and the geometry shown here is why one lesion can imitate the other. Retrograde loss is typically graded — recent years hit hardest, remote memories spared — which is itself an argument that consolidation takes time and that this structure is what performs it.

THE INTERNAL ARCHITECTURE OF THE HIPPOCAMPUS HAS NO MESH AND IS DESCRIBED, NOT DRAWN. Searched across all 934 catalog entries under: dentate, gyrus dentatus, Ammon, cornu, ammonis, CA1, CA3, subiculum, fimbria, alveus, perforant, entorhinal, uncus, hippocampal sulcus. EVERY ONE RETURNS NOTHING. The hippocampus exists only as a single whole-organ mesh per side. Beat 3 therefore states the interlocking Ammon's-horn-and-dentate section in words and says openly that the cut shows one undifferentiated body — including the CA1 sector, which is the part that matters for hypoxic damage and cannot be shown. The FIMBRIA named in beat 5 is likewise not a mesh: the trace runs hippocampus to fornix directly and the narration names the fimbria as the first segment of that road rather than as a lit object.

TWO WIRES OF THE PAPEZ CIRCUIT ARE NAMED AND NOT DRAWN, AND BEAT 6 SAYS SO IN ITS OWN NARRATION. `mammillothalamic`, `cingulum`, `tract` and `bundle` were searched: `tract` returns exactly FOUR entries in the whole catalog — the two iliotibial tracts and the two optic tracts — and there is no mammillothalamic tract and no cingulum. `SHOW_RELATIONSHIP` is used for both links, which is the spec's connector op and does not claim a mesh. The ANTERIOR NUCLEUS of the thalamus is a third described-not-drawn item: `nucleus` in this catalog returns only the caudate nuclei, so the whole thalamus is lit and the narration names which part of it is meant. None of the three is claimed in `covers[]`.

NO ANCHORS WERE AUTHORED AND NONE WAS ATTEMPTED, DELIBERATELY. `tools/derive-landmark.mjs` derives a point ON a parent mesh from contact with a neighbour or from an extreme along an axis. Every feature this scene would want an anchor for — the head of the hippocampus, the fimbria, the uncus, the crus of the fornix — is a REGION of a smooth curved soft-tissue mesh with no attaching neighbour to witness it and no axis that defines it, so neither definition applies and the tool would either refuse or return a number with nothing checking it. The uncus is the closest to measurable (the most medial extreme of the parahippocampal gyrus, `--extreme` on the medial axis) and was still not authored, because 'most medial point of the gyrus' is a proxy for a hook rather than the hook itself and a measured-looking coordinate is believed. Nothing was placed by eye.
